                            THE SECRETARY:    By Senator

                 Little, Legislative Resolution Number 3296,

                 recognizing the 100th Anniversary of The 



                                                        333



                 Post-Star newspaper of Glens Falls, New York.

                            THE PRESIDENT:    Senator Little.

                            SENATOR LITTLE:    Thank you.

                            If I may, I would like to comment

                 on this resolution, which recognizes a local

                 newspaper in my hometown, the Glens Falls

                 Post-Star.

                            The Post-Star began as the Morning 

                 Post in the fall of 1904.  It began as an

                 election campaign newsletter by a group of

                 businessmen.  One of those businessmen later

                 went on to become Governor Dix, who is from

                 Glens Falls.

                            The paper has existed for one

                 hundred years, purchasing other local

                 newspapers and becoming the morning newspaper

                 with a large circulation to the entire greater

                 Glens Falls area.

                            Many notable people have worked for

                 The Post-Star, including our Pulitzer Prize

                 winner, William Kennedy, and our own Senate

                 Majority Leader, Senator Bruno, who was a

                 Post-Star carrier in his youth.

                            We've had many notable

                 publishers -- Arthur P. Irving, a very



                                                        334



                 distinguished Glens Falls resident for many,

                 many years, the publisher of The Post-Star, as

                 well as Karl Davidson.

                            And we are joined today by our

                 current publisher, James Marshall, seated in

                 the gallery, along with our editor, Ken

                 Tingley, with a reporter, Maury Thompson, and

                 long-time Post-Star photographer Monty

                 Calvert.

                            I'm very pleased to have this

                 resolution passed here in the Senate and am

                 joined on the resolution by Senator Bruno and

                 Senator Farley, and certainly wish this

                 newspaper well, having served the community

                 for one hundred years.  And we look forward to

                 another 100 years or 200 years, whatever.

                            It's a long-standing newspaper

                 providing news coverage and community service

                 to our area, and I congratulate them.

                            Thank you.

                            THE PRESIDENT:    Senator Bruno.

                            SENATOR BRUNO:    Thank you, Madam

                 President.  And Senator Little, thank you for

                 introducing the resolution.

                            I want to thank Jim Marshall, Ken



                                                        335



                 Tingley, the managing editor, and Maury

                 Thompson, who reports, for joining us here.

                            This really is something that we

                 do -- and we don't do it just routinely.  When

                 a resolution like this passes, it becomes part

                 of the archives, the history of this state.

                 And it's important that we recognize

                 institutions like The Post-Star, one hundred

                 years old.

                            Now, Betty mentioned some of the

                 notables -- excluding me -- that we're

                 relating -- like Bill Kennedy, Pulitzer Prize.

                 When I was playing in high school, he was

                 associate editor, I believe, there, then went

                 on with The New York Times.

                            And Harold Tanner, who lived on

                 Pearl Street, two blocks from where I lived,

                 Harold distinguished himself.  Harold worked

                 there as a journalist, I think early in his

                 life, went out to make lots of money in the

                 investment banking community, became chairman

                 of the board of Cornell.  Really contributing.

                            But I can tell you this.  The

                 Post-Star had a great effect on my life, for

                 better or for worse.



                                                        336



                            Now, Arthur Irving, in my time, was

                 the publisher.  Arthur Irving -- Betty, do you

                 remember Arthur Irving?  You're a little

                 young.  But Arthur Irving was one of the best

                 citizens in all of the Capital Region and in

                 Glens Falls.  He lived up on Garrison Avenue,

                 a beautiful brick house.  Coincidentally, my

                 brother lives in that house.

                            I went to school with Mary, from

                 kindergarten -- his daughter, Mary Irving, a

                 beautiful lady in every way -- from

                 kindergarten until we graduated together.  And

                 seating was usually that she was here

                 (indicating), because it was the Bs and the Is

                 by rows.  Her brother and Arthur's son,

                 Arthur, I believe went to New York, to The New 

                 York Times, and distinguished himself there.

                 Marsha, the daughter, lives, I believe, out

                 West, not here in the state.

                            But I delivered The Post-Star for

                 about five years, when I was 12, 13, 14, 15,

                 like a lot of young people did.  And now

                 listen to this.  You get up at 6:00 in the

                 morning, 5:30 in the morning, walk seven or

                 eight blocks.  You were on the top of Glen



                                                        337



                 Street.  Were any of you there on top of Glen?

                 You're all in the new building.  You were on

                 top of Glen?  Yeah.

                            Walk there, get the papers, 123,

                 144 papers, fold them.  Today they're either

                 folded or in plastic bags.  We used to have to

                 fold them, stuff them in a bag, lug them, in

                 the middle of the winter, or put them on a

                 bike and deliver it through the whole east

                 end.  That was my route.

                            And I lived about seven or eight

                 blocks from the top of the hill.  I grew up

                 where you are now.  Where they are now is a

                 beautifully renovated train station.  That was

                 the train station.  I lived a block from

                 there, kitty corner.  My brothers delivered

                 The Post-Star.

                            And when I think about The

                 Post-Star, I think about my childhood, I think

                 about my family, I think about all of the

                 things that happened around your newspaper

                 with Arthur Irving.

                            And I know, Jim, you carry on in

                 that tradition of just being good citizens.

                 And I hope you can appreciate how you affect



                                                        338



                 the community's life.

                            Now, I read and Betty told me that

                 you have had more awards since '99 than ever

                 in your previous almost hundred years.  So

                 that shows that there is diligence,

                 conscientiousness, commitment to the community

                 when they get like 17 awards, state and

                 national awards.

                            So, Betty, hopefully they cover you

                 objectively and adequately.

                            I represent South Glens Falls; you

                 have some readership there.  I know my brother

                 and sister get the paper there, and they live

                 there.  Most of my family is still in Glens

                 Falls.  We grew up three or four blocks apart,

                 Betty and I.

                            So I am proud that I am a native of

                 Glens Falls, that you are natives of Glens

                 Falls.  You go back a hundred years.  I don't

                 go back quite a hundred years.  Someday I hope

                 to.

                            (Laughter.)

                            SENATOR BRUNO:    And, David, you'd

                 be happy about that?

                            (Laughter.)



                                                        339



                            SENATOR BRUNO:    So I really just

                 wanted to add a few words to the recognition

                 and the acknowledgement of the great

                 contribution that you make.  Because there

                 isn't anything that goes on that The Post-Star

                 isn't involved in or covering in that

                 community, telling the news, delivering the

                 news, and everyone looking for that paper, and

                 the community service that you perform.

                            So we're indebted to you.  And we

                 welcome the opportunity to say some positive

                 things and to recognize you in a positive way.

                 Congratulations to you.

                            Thank you, Madam President.

                            THE PRESIDENT:    Senator Farley.

                            SENATOR FARLEY:    Thank you, Madam

                 President.

                            I also rise to wish happy birthday

                 to The Post-Star.  Much of my formative years

                 were in Indian Lake, New York.  And we used to

                 visit Glens Falls, and that was going to the

                 big city.  And of course Indian Lake was where

                 The Post-Star was the oracle of truth up that

                 way.

                            And even today, in my Senate



                                                        340



                 district, Corinth and so much of western and

                 northern Saratoga County is serviced by that

                 great newspaper.

                            To last a hundred years in any

                 business is really significant.  And to know

                 that our Majority Leader was a paperboy in

                 Glens Falls is also very significant to

                 everybody in this chamber.

                            But I certainly commend you.  It's

                 still a fine newspaper.  You have a great

                 tradition of history.  A lot of great people

                 came from Glens Falls besides you, Senator

                 Bruno.  Charles Evans Hughes, who ran for

                 president, I think twice, was a Glens Falls

                 native.  So many others who may have been a

                 paper boy for The Post-Star.

                            But at least from my perspective,

                 I'm pleased to be on the resolution and to

                 wish The Post-Star a happy hundredth birthday.

                            Thank you very much.

                            THE PRESIDENT:    All in favor of

                            THE SECRETARY:    Calendar Number

                 54, by Senator Leibell, Senate Print 4815, an

                 act to amend the New York State Urban

                 Development Corporation Act.

                            SENATOR SCHNEIDERMAN:

                 Explanation.

                            THE PRESIDENT:    Senator Bruno.

                            SENATOR BRUNO:    Madam President,

                 I believe Senator Leibell is going to appear

                 momentarily to give an explanation.

                            And there is Senator Leibell to

                 give an explanation.  We applaud Senator

                 Leibell.

                            THE PRESIDENT:    Senator Leibell,

                 an explanation has been requested.



                                                        349



                            SENATOR LEIBELL:    Yes, thank you.

                            Madam President, this bill

                 authorizes the State Urban Development

                 Corporation to enter into a variety of

                 interest-rate exchanges, including

                 fixed-to-floating rate swaps and

                 floating-to-fixed rate swaps.

                            The UDC has had this authority to

                 enter into such exchanges previously and has

                 used it without any incidents.

                            Such authority, however, was viewed

                 as unnecessary due to high stock market

                 conditions and was allowed to sunset in July

                 of 2000.

                            The stock market conditions are

                 still correcting themselves, and the UDC has

                 once again requested this authorization in

                 order to save the state money on its

                 investment capital.

                            Interest-rate exchange agreements

                 can result in much lower net cost of

                 borrowing, reduce the financial exposure of

                 the corporation, or reduce the corporation's

                 exposure to changes in interest rates in a

                 particular financial transaction.



                                                        350



                            If we were to enact this

                 legislation, it would save substantial money

                 for the state.

                            This bill did pass last year in the

                 Senate, 61 to 1.

                            THE PRESIDENT:    Senator Krueger.

                            SENATOR LIZ KRUEGER:    Madam

                 President, if, through you, the sponsor would

                 yield.

                            THE PRESIDENT:    Senator Leibell,

                 do you yield for a question?

                            SENATOR LEIBELL:    Yes, I do.

                            THE PRESIDENT:    Go ahead, Senator

                 Krueger.

                            SENATOR LIZ KRUEGER:    Thank you,

                 Madam President.

                            We had this discussion last year

                 when the bill was brought to the floor, so I

                 don't want to necessarily reenact my whole

                 series of questions.

                            But last year I had the concern, as

                 I do now, that these are technically swaps or

                 even derivative arrangements and these are

                 considered in the financial markets as what

                 are called high-risk types of investments.



                                                        351



                            And if we are asking or we are

                 giving an off-budget authority, the UDC, the

                 authority to go into these kinds of financial

                 arrangements, what kind of protections or

                 limits would this legislation set on ensuring,

                 one, that somebody is managing these in a way

                 that they are tracking, extremely carefully,

                 these high-risk investments?

                            And, two, are they -- I guess I'll

                 make it two questions, Madam President, if the

                 sponsor doesn't mind.  And, two, are there any

                 limits set on how much the UDC could put into

                 these interest-rate exchanges or swaps?

                            Because in the past, in past years

                 when Governor Pataki had proposed this model,

                 he had actually said in his capital plans and

                 debt service analysis that these are

                 considered higher-risk types of investments

                 and only a limited amount of state debt should

                 ever be allowed to be invested this way.

                            SENATOR LEIBELL:    With respect to

                 the amount, the market really does control

                 that.

                            With respect to categorizing this

                 as a high risk, indications we've had is that



                                                        352



                 there are always going to be varieties of risk

                 and different levels of risk, but that this is

                 not a great risk.  It's been done many times

                 in many places before.  It's done in the

                 private sector.

                            This is something that is viewed as

                 having a limited utility but, to the extent

                 that it is utilized, it will save the state

                 substantial monies.

                            SENATOR LIZ KRUEGER:    Thank you,

                 Madam President.  Briefly on the bill.

                            THE PRESIDENT:    You may proceed

                 on the bill, Senator.

                            SENATOR LIZ KRUEGER:    Thank you.

                            I appreciate Senator Leibell's

                 answer to my questions, but I want to clarify

                 that I do think that this is a high-risk type

                 of investment.  And when you read through

                 various analyses of the types of debts that

                 states take on, in fact, swaps, derivatives,

                 interest-rate changes are defined by the

                 market as a very volatile type of investment,

                 and there is risk involved.

                            It is quite a few years now since

                 Orange County went bankrupt over swaps and



                                                        353



                 derivatives arrangements, and there have been

                 some protections built into the market.  But

                 as I believe the Senator said himself in his

                 opening presentation, the market is still

                 adjusting itself.

                            And the concern in this market is

                 that it is volatile.  We discover each day

                 that there is exposure of various corporations

                 to having not provided accurate information to

                 the public or to government, and there are

                 still investigations going on by the SEC and

                 by our own Attorney General Eliot Spitzer as

                 to some of the behavior of some investment

                 corporations.

                            And I am very concerned that

                 New York State should not be investing our

                 money in high-risk types of investments, even

                 though it is true with a high risk can come a

                 high reward.  You can see higher earnings, but

                 you could also take a higher risk of losing

                 your capital in this type of investment.

                            And I am also particularly

                 concerned that this bill doesn't set any

                 limits on how much the UDC might be investing

                 in this type of financial vehicle.  It doesn't



                                                        354



                 set any mandate on what kind of oversight must

                 be applied.

                            When the Comptroller of the State

                 of New York invests state money for a variety

                 of reasons, there's an entire institutional

                 structure and a series of rules that are

                 applied about the investment of New York State

                 monies.

                            But I don't believe that the UDC,

                 as an off-budget authority, was set up for

                 this purpose or has anywhere near the type of

                 institutional structure in place to watch this

                 volatile market and these types of volatile

                 investments carefully or carefully enough for

                 the people of New York State.

                            So I do understand that, again,

                 with a higher risk might come a higher return,

                 which might save the people of New York State

                 money over time.  I think that the risks are

                 greater than the reward in this situation and

                 that as a state we should be relatively

                 conservative with our investment strategies,

                 particularly because we have lost so much

                 money in the last few years in the market.

                 And these are again, I think, still considered



                                                        355



                 volatile and even risky investments.

                            Michigan, for example, does allow

                 some of its money to be invested using swaps

                 or derivatives, but they have a very carefully

                 laid out statute about what can and cannot be

                 done, how much can be invested, what kind of

                 oversight, what the role of the governing body

                 must be, and even something called swap

                 management plans and debt management plans for

                 evaluating this.

                            I don't believe that this

                 legislation as it's being presented offers any

                 of those models.

                            And again, to allow off-budget

                 authorities the kind of power that they

                 already have, plus the ability to now walk

                 into volatile market arrangements, would not

                 be in the best interests of the State of

                 New York.  Even though it is true in some

                 short-term scenario we might see a higher

                 return, we could also see a significant loss

                 or even default on these monies.

                            So while I don't claim to be the

                 world's expert on interest-rate swaps or

                 derivatives, I have done enough homework to



                                                        356



                 convince myself that this is considered a

                 relatively high-risk venture in finance and

                 it's not what we should be allowing any

                 off-budget authority in New York State to be

                 taking on for itself with our money.

                            So I will be voting no against your

                 bill again this year.

                            Thank you very much, Madam

                 President.

                            SENATOR SCHNEIDERMAN:    Thank you,

                 Madam President.  On the bill.



                                                        357



                            THE PRESIDENT:    You may proceed,

                 Senator.

                            SENATOR SCHNEIDERMAN:    I think

                 that while there may be some disagreement as

                 to the degree of risk in these particular

                 can agree that there is substantial risk to

                 continue to allow public benefit corporations

                 and authorities to operate the way they are

                 operating now.

                 authorities.  We have dozens of other smaller

                 ones.  We have a system of off-book

                 recordkeeping and financing that really is as

                 intricate and opaque as anything that has been

                 state level.

                            There is no excuse, for those of us

                 who are public servants and are responsible

                 for supervising the expenditure of public

                 funds, for us to allow year after year this

                 situation to get worse and worse.



                                                        358



                            And it's really something that cuts

                 against the entire principle of public

                 authorities.  Although they were originally

                 enacted to provide something that was beyond

                 politics, we find that we have very few things

                 more political and less subject to scrutiny

                 than the public authorities in this state.

                            Senator Paterson has introduced

                 legislation to deal with this.  There is

                 legislation in the Assembly.  And I think that

                 the points that Senator Krueger is making

                 carrying more debt than all but a few states

                 in the entire country.

                            It's time to get that back in line.

                 series of scandals and a collapse in the

                 state's bond ratings occasioned by the
